turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Sunday, the twenty-fifth of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Israel sealed Hebron and displaced about two thousand Palestinians, three days before a national vote.
Europe once published a number that let you compare two vacuum cleaners. A court annulled it, and nobody ever replaced it.
And archery, where a dozen arrows cost more than the bow.
[curious] More than the bow?

More than the bow. Hold that. Saturday the twenty-fourth. Israel's army sealed Hebron and began a closure of the occupied West Bank, a day after two soldiers were shot dead at a checkpoint outside the city.
Two soldiers. Both killed?
Both. [thoughtful] Two attackers were killed as well. Then about two thousand people were emptied from their neighbourhoods, and they go to the polls — or don't — on Tuesday.
Wait. The closure runs through the election?

That's the shape of it. Prime Minister Netanyahu ordered it within hours. His words: he'd instructed the army and security forces to immediately impose a closure on the city of Hebron. On how many were displaced, two counts are printed and they don't agree. Defence Minister Katz said about two thousand had been displaced and would not be allowed back until the army finishes with Hamas in Hebron. Hebron's mayor counts two thousand two hundred forced out.
That's close enough to be the same event and far enough apart to matter.

Both are printed. Palestinian officials add another two thousand five hundred evacuations. The governorate holds roughly eight hundred thousand people. The sceptic's line is that the timing reads as an inference, not a confession. Netanyahu cancelled all his party events on Friday, promised the Palestinian Authority a big surprise on Saturday, and said the army is ready to execute and we will set the timing.
[skeptical] Which is suggestive. It isn't proof.

It isn't. The test is simple — if the closure lifts before Tuesday, the timing argument weakens. Watch that. On the demolitions — one report that Israel's High Court had cleared them couldn't be confirmed in four reads of the Israeli live blogs. So it's named here, and not printed as fact. One more number. Four hundred and nine attacks on Palestinian farmers, land and olive trees in October alone — seventeen of them on Thursday.
Four hundred and nine in a month.
In twenty-three days.
The other thing on the World pages is the Meta judgment, and it's almost funny.
A New Mexico judge cut Meta's penalty from two hundred and nineteen billion dollars to twenty-five billion.
[laughs] Cut. That's a word doing a lot of work.
A jury had found forty-three million eight hundred and ninety-nine thousand violations of the state's Unfair Practices Act, at five thousand dollars each.
Multiply it out and you get —
Two hundred and nineteen billion. The judgment says it is reduced to the amount of twenty-five billion. And it gives no method.
None at all?
None. What it gives is a rate — fifteen per cent a year until paid in full. That's roughly three point seven five billion a year. About ten point three million dollars a day.
[exhales] So the interest is the real sentence.

One analyst says Meta is worth nearly two trillion and will likely keep appealing these cases and drag them out. Meta's own counsel says nobody in New Mexico heard or saw the statements at issue. The quarterly filing confirms the order and says the company intends to appeal. It also says it has accrued an amount — and won't say how much.
[wry] So twenty-five billion is a ceiling, not a cost.
That's exactly the line. Not a measure of it.
Money block. What did the week actually do?
Traders pushed the ten-year below five per cent on Thursday. Nineteen point three basis points down to four point nine five three — the steepest one-day fall since March two thousand twenty-three.
Why?

Meta's results and a widening in artificial-intelligence-linked credit spreads. Money went into government debt. That was the first close below five per cent since the twenty-second of September. Then Friday undid half of it — reports that the United States and Israel were weighing renewed strikes on Iran. Brent up three point one four per cent to one hundred and sixteen dollars seventy-two — its highest since April.
Shares and yields both up on Friday?

Both. Which is the oil-shock signature — not a barrel of crude so much as a growth scare, then a handover. And the diversification trade — the week's real question — finally worked. The world-equity proxy fell one point zero eight per cent while the global-aggregate bond proxy rose nought point one seven. First time in this cycle where the bond leg offset a world-equity drawdown rather than compounding it. Gold we print as a band, not a point. Three thousand nine hundred and ninety-four to four thousand and eight US dollars. Four venues, no agreement, one with the opposite sign.
[deadpan] So we didn't quietly pick one.
We didn't quietly pick one. And none of this is a buy or sell call.
Singapore. The price print.
Core inflation eased to two point zero per cent year on year in September, from two point two in August. Headline two point two, from two point three.
Which sounds like good news until you open the table.
Electricity and gas have run eight point seven per cent dearer a year for three straight months. Private transport is seven point one.
[sighs] So the thing that eased is services and retail.
And here's the arithmetic. Electricity and gas carry one hundred and ninety-eight points of the ten-thousand-point basket. Accommodation carries two thousand six hundred and fifty-six.
So an eight point seven rise can sit next to a two point two headline —

— because the index isn't weighted by how much it annoys you. We recomputed that from the statistics department's own table. And what people expect is more than the print. A survey of five hundred and ten residents, fielded in September, puts one-year-ahead headline at three point four per cent. One-year core, three point six.
Against a two point zero actual.
Against two point zero.
Technology, and this is where the issue finds its shape.
The United States Treasury filed a thirty-eight page proposed rule on Friday morning that would forbid Americans from funding the development of any super intelligence system in six countries.
And the number it uses to decide what that is?
Ten to the twenty-fifth computational operations of training.
[curious] Which is the only number in the whole programme.
Was. Treasury proposes to delete it. Its own preamble says no single measure, benchmark, or threshold is currently sufficient to distinguish advanced models.
Which is — true, actually.

It's true. Sparse architectures, post-training technique, inference-time compute. A sparse model that activates twenty-three billion of four hundred and twenty-eight billion parameters breaks the proxy by construction.
[thoughtful] So they're right, and they fixed it by removing the measurement.

[pause] That's the issue's spine, and you just said it. The thing that was fixed was not the thing that was broken. Two practitioners are quoted on it. One calls it just the first step in a fairly long process. Another says it will require more substantial compliance programmes. Both are relayed through an outlet our desk couldn't open, and we say so on the page. Comments close on the seventh of December.
Okay, the Home Lab, because this one's genuinely good.
MiniMax published open weights for a four hundred and twenty-eight billion parameter model on Friday. Within hours the main local runtime was emitting fluent nonsense.
[laughs] Fluent nonsense is the worst kind.
It is. No error. No warning. Prompted with the capital of France is, it returned unrelated tokens in four scripts.
And everyone blamed their own quantisation.

Everyone blamed their own quantisation. The cause was one layer down. It's a mixed-precision model — one format for the routed experts, another for the dense weights — and the graph file never handed the runtime the per-expert quantisation scales.
So the loader read them —
— read them off disk correctly, and then never passed them down. Nine tensors. Every expert weight came out at its default, roughly fifteen thousand times too large.
[gasps] Fifteen thousand times.

And attention and the prediction head were scaled properly, so the residual stream stayed valid at every layer and merely drowned. No assertion fires. No not-a-number. The model loads at plausible speed and writes fluent nonsense. A maintainer merged the nine-tensor fix a day later. [wry] One day. And the only throughput anyone has measured — five point one two tokens a second, on a consumer card with a hundred and twenty-eight gigabytes of system memory.
One number.
One number, for a model with fifteen published benchmark scores — and it came from the bug report, not the vendor. No measured memory figure exists from any source.
The Kit.

Grado opened pre-orders on Thursday for the Signature S one fifty, at two hundred and ninety-five US dollars. In that line it is the cheapest open-back they've ever put in the Signature range by a long way. The next one up is nine hundred and ninety-five. The flagship is two thousand four hundred and ninety-five.
So it undercuts the model directly above it by about —

Seventy per cent. New forty-four millimetre paper-composite driver, two hundred and twenty grams, thirty-eight ohms, detachable cable for the first time down here. The measurements? [deadpan] There are none, and that's the story. Three days after pre-orders opened, the main measurement forum's search returns no results found. No measurement thread exists. The news aggregator has nothing.
So what's the one figure that earns its ink?
Nought point zero five decibels of driver matching. It says the pairs are hand-matched. Everything else on the page is frequency response.
[chuckles] Which is the number nobody can hear and everybody prints.
And one sceptic, an engineer at a rival, says it is premature to assume the cheap one delivers the same level of refinement — and notes he is borrowing their design ideas.
Honest of him.
Unusually.
The Atelier. Vacuum cleaners, which I did not expect to enjoy.

Start with the mechanism, because it's two numbers that can't both be true at once. Water lift is measured at a sealed orifice, where airflow is zero. Airflow is measured wide open, where lift is almost nothing.
[curious] So the peak is in the middle.

The peak is in the middle. One commodity motor pulls one hundred and forty-five point six inches of water sealed and moves nothing at all; wide open it moves one hundred and three point two cubic feet a minute. Peak power is neither — it's about five hundred and twenty-one air watts.
And a box figure quotes whichever end flatters the machine.

Whichever end flatters the machine. So Europe published a comparable number — and then stopped. Dyson argued the test was run with an empty bag, so bagged machines, whose pores clog in use, were flattered. The court agreed in November two thousand eighteen.
And because the calculation couldn't be severed —
The whole regulation fell. From the eighteenth of January two thousand nineteen it was void as if it had never existed.
[exhales] As if it had never existed.

And nothing has replaced it. What survives is a floor, not a ladder: since two thousand seventeen a vacuum sold in Europe must do five hundred motor hours, lift seventy-five per cent of test dust from carpet, and re-emit under one per cent.
A floor every honest maker already clears.
One maker claims a thousand hours. The commodity motor anyone can order by part number claims fifteen hundred.
So the premium is not the motor.

Cordless is the step that is not an upgrade, either. One maker's cordless costs more than its own corded flagship, carries two years instead of five, and excludes battery run-time from the warranty. Next on the bench: table linen, hand planes and chisels, and mosquito nets.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every week.
Every week. Archery. Tell me about the arrows.

One line from a catalogue. At one shop on Friday, a dozen top-tier shafts were four hundred and ninety-nine dollars ninety-nine. A serious competition riser was three hundred and ninety-nine ninety-nine.
So the thing you hold costs less than the things you throw away.
And the things you throw away are the consumable. Beginners spend months choosing a bow and then shoot it with whatever arrows came in the bundle.
Why does a systems person fall into this?

Because it's a tunable machine with a legible output and exactly one unreliable part. Spine, centre-shot, brace height, tiller, front-of-centre — all adjustable, all interacting. The output is a score out of seven hundred and twenty. No judging panel.
And the unreliable part is —
You. Which is why the premium end of the market is mostly devices for taking decisions away from the person holding the bow.
[amused] That's the whole hobby in one sentence.

Now the part I didn't expect. Spine — arrow stiffness — is the most argued-about number in the sport. You hang eight hundred and eighty grams at the middle of a shaft supported twenty-eight inches apart and read the bend. Simple enough, except for three problems. An older standard used a two-pound weight over twenty-six inches, so spine is one word for two different measurements.
[sighs] Of course it is.
Second: the formal test method was marked historical and its revision withdrawn in two thousand twenty-three. The parameters sit behind a paywall.
Withdrawn. So there's no current standard.

And third — static spine can't predict what the arrow actually does. Dynamic spine depends on point weight, insert mass, fletching and the bow's acceleration. The other foundational number is draw weight. The weight stamped on a limb is its pull at twenty-eight inches, and draw length is defined as nock point to the grip's pivot plus one and three-quarter inches.
Where's that written down?
[deadpan] The trade association's technical guidelines. Members only.
[laughs] So both of archery's defining numbers are specified in documents the archer can't read.
That's the sentence the page is built on. Then the price spread. A sprung pin called a plunger. One costs four dollars fifty. Another costs one hundred and ninety-nine ninety-nine. Forty-four times.
For a pin.

The expensive one's spare thread cylinder alone is ninety-four ninety-nine. And the makers quietly ended their own longest argument. Foam core versus wood core — one house sells both at exactly the same price. Another sells carbon-foam and carbon-wood at exactly the same price. Neither will say one is better.
Because they aren't.
Because they won't claim it. Meanwhile there's a graphene limb whose page never says what the graphene contributes, and a riser sold on a clicker whose felt impulse is increased fifty-five per cent.
[laughs] A marketing claim about an auditory cue.

A marketing claim about an auditory cue. And Singapore changed sixteen months ago, and almost nothing written online predates it. A bow meeting international target specification is a Type Two weapon under a class licence. Anything heavier is Type One, and not allowed to individuals. Heavier means above sixty pounds of draw — which for recurve is no constraint at all — competition limbs run twenty-eight to fifty. Compound is commonly specified forty to seventy.
So when you order compound limbs here —
Specify fifty or sixty. Never seventy.
[thoughtful] And target panic. That's the human bit.
It's not a fringe affliction. It's a product category. The world number one compound archer in two thousand eighteen twitched at full draw on his last two arrows and shot a six.
Oof.

His words: it's called target panic, and it's not fun. And the gear sold against it: a hinge release that rotates past a sear. A resistance release that fires when back tension crosses a threshold. Neither lets the archer choose the instant of the shot.
[thoughtful] So you buy the decision out of your own hands.
That's what the money is for. Next descents: violin making, competitive barbecue, and astrophotography on a budget.
Culture. The film everyone's arguing about.

A documentary about Elizabeth Holmes took six point one million dollars across two thousand six hundred and fifty-five North American theatres on Friday. Second place — to a studio comic-book picture that opened above it with ten point four million on three thousand four hundred and fifty-eight screens. And now the scores, which are the real story. Ninety-eight per cent on one aggregator from one hundred and sixty-six critics. Ninety-seven on the other — from forty.
[curious] Forty.
Two panels, the same film, the same week, differing fourfold in sample size. The higher-sounding number is the fragile one.
The Good Life.

A New York micro-brand launched a titanium watch on Saturday at seven thousand seven hundred US dollars. One hundred and eighty-eight plain-dial pieces, plus twelve diamond-set at nine thousand seven hundred. Inside is the same movement that already powers their standard model at six thousand three hundred.
So the premium for the engraving is —
Fourteen hundred dollars. Twenty-two per cent, for surface work alone.
[wry] Which is either outrageous or exactly the point.

The pattern is naval dazzle camouflage — the scheme that never tried to hide a ship, only to make it hard to read. And the maker's own writer at one publication will not endorse the watch he's introducing. He says the look isn't totally to my taste, and that he wouldn't rank it among his favourite releases.
[laughs] In the launch piece.
In the launch piece.
The Family Desk. The phone ban study.
Dutch secondary schools. One thousand three hundred and ninety-eight students. Full bans compared against partial bans on every wellbeing measure a ban is meant to improve.
And?

Nothing moved. Life satisfaction, loneliness, physical complaints, fatigue, emotional complaints — the authors' own summary is that no significant differences were found for any of the wellbeing or bullying outcomes.
[thoughtful] And something did move.
Student-teacher connectedness fell under the full ban. For girls more than boys.
So the stricter policy did nothing it was for, and damaged something it wasn't.
That's the finding. And it published on the seventh of January, the same month Singapore extended its own restriction to the whole school day.
Which is the issue's spine again.

The wrong layer. Yes. And Fitness lands in the same place. Twenty-five adults with moderate-to-severe sleep apnoea. Eight weeks of resistance training, three sessions a week. Self-rated sleep quality improved by three point two points.
And the thing a patient actually complains about?
Daytime sleepiness. Measured on the one validated scale. No significant difference.
[sighs] So the headline won't carry.
The headline won't carry. And the mean age is fifty-four point six, with a mean body-mass index of thirty-six point one.
Which is not a twenty-five-year-old lifting.
Not even close. General guidance, not medical advice — talk to a doctor before changing how you train.
And the Diary, quickly.

Studio Ghibli opens at Gardens by the Bay on the eighteenth of December. Resident tickets thirty-nine dollars adult, twenty-nine concession, early bird to the seventeenth. But the date to actually diarise is the fifth of December. Advance sale for January's Tokyo sumo tournament. November's is already sold out on every day, with no same-day sales. And the rail pass resolved. The official site still sells the seven-day online at fifty thousand yen while a designated agent abroad charges fifty-three.
[curious] The old price is still there?
Still there. Buy online, from Japan's own site, and you're paying last month's price. How long that lasts, nobody will say.
The Undercurrent.

New Zealand freed a thing called papakāinga — clustered housing on ancestral Māori land — from planning law. Since July, ten homes per site, no resource consent, overriding every district plan in the country.
That's real.
That's real, and it was overdue, and it is genuinely gone as an obstacle.
[thoughtful] But.

But the binding constraint was never zoning. It's title. A law from eighteen sixty-five converted communal land into individual freehold shares, and those shares pass to heirs in equal undivided fractions.
And never consolidate.

Never. A hundred and sixty-one years later, twenty-seven thousand titles carry three and a quarter million ownership interests. The average block has fifty-three hectares and one hundred and fourteen owners.
No bank lends against that.

No bank takes it as security. So the house has to be the collateral — which means building on piles, not a slab, at an extra forty to fifty thousand dollars, before a bank's ordinary credit test even starts. And the test case is brutal. One of the country's fastest-growing cities issued sixteen code compliance certificates for homes on Māori land in five years. Sixteen. Against thousands built across the city in the same period.
[whispers] Sixteen.
And the number of owners per block has risen in every year anyone has published. Ninety-six in twenty thirteen. One hundred and fourteen in twenty twenty-four.
So the ratchet keeps turning underneath the reform.

Here's the comparison that earns its keep. The United States did exactly the same thing in eighteen eighty-seven — divided tribal land into individual parcels, same stated purpose, same intestate succession, same result.
And then?
And then spent real money undoing it. A one point nine billion dollar fund that spent a decade buying fractional interests back from willing sellers and returning them to tribal ownership.
[exhales] They treated the title as the problem.
They treated the title as the problem and bought it back. [pause] New Zealand amended the zoning.
Is that unfair?

The fairest objection is that it undersells a real reform, and it has force. Most of the land area is already vested in a management structure. And finance is being fixed in parallel — a loan cap raised from two hundred thousand to five hundred thousand a dwelling.
So it isn't nothing.
It isn't nothing. But the layer underneath is still compounding — about ninety-six owners a block, then a hundred and fourteen — and nothing in the new regulations touches it.
[thoughtful] One academic put it well, didn't she.
He. We know from experience that planning reform alone does not build homes.
[pause] And the houses that do get built?
[warmly] Will be real. So will the ones that don't.
That's the thread of the whole issue, isn't it. Repairs made at the layer that's reachable.
A threshold deleted rather than improved. A bug one layer below the one everyone blamed. A label annulled and never replaced. A ban that moved nothing it aimed at.
[warmly] And a planning law rewritten over a title nobody will lend against.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
